name: Computer Vision Inspection
blurb: AI inspection of tablets, vials and packaging on the line.
title: Computer Vision Inspection
answer: AI vision systems inspect products on high speed lines and detect subtle defects older rule based systems miss, such as cracks, particles and print errors. Because they make or support release relevant decisions, they need the same validation as other inspection equipment, with a defined defect library and challenge sets.

reading.body:
AI vision inspection earns its place on a pharmaceutical line by catching cracks, particles and print errors that fixed-rule systems miss, but it only counts once it is validated like any other inspection equipment.

The pattern is that the hard part is not detection, it is proof. A deep learning model learns defects from labelled images and tolerates natural variation better than fixed rules, which reduces false rejects, the good units thrown away for nothing. That gain is only real if the system is challenged: a defect library covering every defect type, challenge sets of known good and bad units, predefined detection and false reject criteria, and requalification after any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product.

This matters for AI because inspection sits on release decisions, so the model is not a convenience, it is equipment. Locked models and traceable decisions are what let it fit current GMP and draft Annex 22. The compute here is modest and runs at line speed, so the binding constraint is governance and requalification effort, not power or buildings.

What the data does not cover is cost, throughput numbers, error rates, or any named regulator position beyond the reference to draft Annex 22. It also gives one 2024 study as the only dated development, so it establishes that the capability exists and how it must be controlled, not how widely it is deployed.

The mechanism that separates a working vision system from a validated one is the challenge set, not the model. A deep learning model learns defects from labelled images and tolerates natural variation better than fixed rules, which is why false rejects fall. But the same flexibility that lets it accept harmless variation also lets it drift, so the defect library and the challenge set are what convert a detection capability into an inspection decision you can defend.

The comparison the data supports is between two failure modes, not two technologies. Fixed rules produce false rejects, good units thrown away for nothing. A model that is never challenged produces the opposite risk, a defect that passes because nothing in the validation ever asked it to catch that defect. The data names only the first failure mode explicitly and defines the second only through the challenge set requirement.

The practical consequence is that requalification is a recurring cost, not a one-time gate. Any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product triggers a rerun of the challenge set, so the effort scales with how often the line changes rather than with how much compute the model needs. That is why the binding constraint here is governance and requalification effort, not power or buildings.

What is a false reject?
A good unit wrongly rejected as defective, which wastes product without improving quality.

How is an AI inspection system challenged?
By running it on a set of known defective and good units and confirming it meets predefined criteria.

What has to be in place before a vision system can support a release decision?
A defect library covering all defect types, challenge sets of known good and bad units, predefined detection and false reject criteria, and requalification after any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product.

When does a validated vision system have to be requalified?
After any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product.

Does the data give throughput, error rates or cost figures for these systems?
No. The data does not hold throughput numbers, error rates or cost figures.

What evidence does the data give that this capability actually works?
One 2024 study in Scientific Reports demonstrating deep learning based defect detection for pharmaceutical quality control in real time. The data gives no deployment counts beyond that.

explainer:
Visual inspection checks products for defects: cracked or chipped tablets, foreign particles in vials, fill level, seal integrity, label and print errors. Manual inspection is tiring and inconsistent, and traditional automated systems use fixed rules that struggle with natural variation, producing false rejects that waste good product.

Deep learning vision systems learn what defects look like from labelled images and can distinguish real defects from harmless variation more reliably. Because inspection supports release decisions, validation is essential: a defect library covering all defect types, challenge sets of known good and bad units, predefined detection and false reject criteria, and requalification after any change to the model, cameras, lighting or product. Locked models and full traceability of decisions fit both current GMP and draft Annex 22.

What vision systems inspect

Cameras have checked pharmaceutical products for decades: particles in vials, cracks in glass, cap seals, tablet defects, label text and barcodes, and the completeness of packs. Traditional systems use rules set by engineers, which work well for defects that look the same every time and poorly for ones that vary. Machine learning inspection learns from examples of good and defective product, which lets it catch irregular defects and adapt to new products faster, and it can grade severity rather than only pass or fail.

Why it is a quality decision

An inspection system that rejects a vial or passes a tablet is making a release decision about product that will reach a patient. That places it firmly inside the quality system. The model has to be validated against a library of defects, including rare and subtle ones, with evidence of how often it misses true defects and how often it rejects good product. Its performance has to be monitored because lighting, camera wear and product changes shift what the images look like. And every rejection has to be traceable, because batch records and investigations depend on it.

The practical gains and the limits

Plants report fewer false rejects, which saves product, and more consistent detection than human inspectors, who tire. Some run machine learning alongside rule based systems and human review during a transition, which generates the comparison data regulators like to see. The limit is the defect library: a model cannot catch a defect type it has never seen, so plants keep collecting and labelling examples, and they keep people in the loop for anything the model flags as uncertain.
